newsitem.title: USA: Mass. Gov. proposes new revenue bonding authority.
newsitem.headline: Mass. Gov. proposes new revenue bonding authority.

text.p: Massachusetts Gov. William F. Weld proposed Tuesday a new bonding authority with revenues coming from the Massachusetts Turnpike and Boston's tunnels.
The proposal, however, has raised credit concerns, especially among bond raters.
Gov. Weld is proposing to use the tolls and revenues from air rights to offset the state's share of the Central Artery, or Big Dig, project.

The Metropolitan Highway System (MHS), proposed to the legislature Tuesday, would help pay for Boston's $10.4 billion Central Artery Third Harbor Tunnel project, the biggest public works program in the country.
The MHS would include that portion of the Massachusetts Turnpike closest to Boston, as well as the Sumner and Callahan Tunnels.
And the MHS would also have bonding authority.
The Massachusetts Turnpike Authority would continue to oversee the turnpike west of route 128.

"At this point we can't tell if they'll be better off or worse off. This new MHS could change completely the configuration of the authority. We'll look at protection of current bond holders," said Chee Mee Hu, vice president of Moody's Investors Service.
If a the MHS is created by carving out part of the turnpike, the agreement between currentbond holders and the turnpike would be violated, Hu said.
"They've issued debt based on the current structure backed by tolls,'' Hu said. New bonds would have to be issued, she said.
It is difficult to assess whether Massachusetts' plan is a sound one until the federal government acts and a definitive financing plan is provided by state officials, Hu said.
The federal government is expected to pick up between 15 percent and 50 percent of the cost of the Big Dig. Congress will decide the portion later this year.

Neither Administration and Finance Secretary Charlie Baker nor Transportation Secretary James Kerasiotes could say how much revenue would flow to the Big Dig project from the tolls and air rights of the MHS.
In the past, Kerasiotes has referred to the Turnpike as a "cash cow."

Still, many lawmakers and tax experts were concerned when the Republican governor, who last year was in a fierce contest to win the seat of U.S. Sen. John F. Kerry, a Democrat, eliminated four tolls at the Western most end of the state.

That action violated the Turnpike Authority's agreement with its bondholders, so Moody's felt compelled to inform Wall Street, even though the agency did not feel that the authority's fiscal health was in danger, Hu said.
"The authority produces nice revenues," Hu said.
The state currently has a self-imposed bond cap of $900 million for all projects.

Kerasiotes and Baker insisted that Legislators Tuesday said that they would act quickly on the MHS proposal, although some concerns were expressed that new borrowing not impact the state's current ambitious road and bridge program.
That program was halted last year for a number of months when when the state exceeded its self-imposed bond cap of $900 million.
--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
